entry.title: A Bayesian-Geometric Reading of Classical Model-Based Optimal Design

link.title: A Bayesian-Geometric Reading of Classical Model-Based Optimal Design

entry.content:
The classical model-based optimal design criteria (D-, T-, L-, C-, and A-optimality) are usually motivated via the Cram'er–Rao bound as optimizing scalar functions of the Fisher information matrix (FIM). This paper offers a complementary reading in which each criterion appears asymptotically as $N \to \infty$ as the leading-order term of an expected dissimilarity between prior and posterior, with the FIM entering through the Bernstein–von Mises limit. The Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of the posterior relative to the prior recovers D-optimality (classically known); a reverse KL of the prior relative to the posterior recovers T-optimality (here defined as maximization of the trace of the FIM, following one common convention) and its weighted-trace generalization; and a first-order approximation of the squared 2-Wasserstein distance recovers L-, C- and A-optimality. The five criteria emerge as instances of a common Bayesian-geometric template, indexed by three choices: the dissimilarity, the prior parametrization, and the approximation scheme used to evaluate it (e.g.\ Taylor expansions of the matrix square root). For the weighted criteria, the Gaussian prior covariance encodes the criterion’s weight matrix, so any choice of weights corresponds to a specific prior in the family. The T-, L-, C-, and A-optimality derivations appear novel to the best of my knowledge. A sixth criterion, E-optimality, is recovered not as an independent expected-dissimilarity limit but as a min-max robustification of C-optimality against uncertainty in the modeler’s prior direction. The framework is extended to distinguish between a designer’s prior over unknown parameters at design time and a modeler’s prior used for posterior inference, recovering the classical expected information gain objective as a special case.

entry.title: A Layered Simplex Architecture for Large Alphabets

link.title: A Layered Simplex Architecture for Large Alphabets

entry.content:
A learning architecture induces a prior over its expressible models. Recent work links architectural success to a broad complexity spectrum: model probabilities spanning many orders of magnitude. Understanding how depth shapes these priors and prediction may help explain the success of neural networks and transformers. We study this connection in large-alphabet prediction through the layered simplex architecture (LSA), which multiplies independent uniform simplex vectors coordinate-wise and normalizes. At depth zero, the prior is concentrated on the uniform distribution; at depth one, the Bayesian predictor is Laplace’s rule. Each additional layer shifts prior mass toward more concentrated distributions. We derive exact Bayesian marginal likelihood and regret expressions using reusable depth-specific kernels. Mixing over depths up to a cutoff logarithmic in alphabet size yields an explicit predictor with rigorous guarantees. For targets uniform on a specified sparse support, the mixture’s prior complexity is asymptotic to the support-description cost at every fixed positive KL resolution, establishing a broad complexity spectrum. We also prove a regret lower bound for every label-invariant predictor: the expected description length of the discovered symbol set minus the source’s uncertainty about its identity given its size. For Zipf sources in a growing-alphabet regime, the depth mixture attains this bound to leading order. Thus, the symbol-discovery rate determines the regret exponent. Although introduced to study depth, the LSA predictor competes with established large-alphabet methods, including Good–Turing, Ristad’s law and an adaptive Dirichlet mixture, while substantially outperforming classical add-constant rules on concentrated sources.

entry.title: A Probabilistic Framework for Estimating the Modal Age at Death

link.title: A Probabilistic Framework for Estimating the Modal Age at Death

entry.content:
The modal age at death is used to track longevity, but existing methods report it as a single number. We estimate its posterior distribution. Death counts are modeled as Poisson given the death rates and exposures, and posterior draws of the rates, passed through the life table, give the probability that each age is the mode and a credible interval for an interpolated modal age. With independent gamma priors, the posterior is computed exactly and concentrates on the true mode as the population grows. Because single-year rates are noisy, we also use a second-order random-walk prior on the log rates, which shares information across neighboring ages and estimates the degree of smoothing from the data; this posterior is computed with a Laplace approximation, which we check against posterior sampling. In simulations, the random-walk posterior mean was 1.4 to 10.6 times more accurate than the posterior mean under independent priors. When the distribution of deaths was unimodal, its errors were close to those of P-spline and Gompertz estimates, which were slightly more accurate; with a secondary peak, P-splines were the most accurate. The random-walk credible intervals were conservative, covering the true mode in 98% to 100% of replications, whereas bootstrap intervals for the other estimators either covered it less often or were much wider. For women in Denmark, France, Japan and Sweden since 1960, the random-walk estimates hardly changed with the starting age of the estimation, and the posterior gives the probability that the modal age declined in 2020.

entry.title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding

link.title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding

entry.content:
We study a fundamental problem in machine learning: partial recovery of a planted signal $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ from a spiked tensor $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{X}} = \lambda \, \boldsymbol{v}^{\otimes p} + \boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$, where $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ has symmetric Gaussian entries of variance $\asymp n^{-1}$. While previous works replace $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ by an i.i.d. standard Gaussian tensor to circumvent technical difficulties caused by dependencies, this paper directly analyzes the symmetric model via random matrix theory. We show that the square unfolding algorithm is subject to a sharp phase transition for partial recovery at $\lambda \asymp n^{(p-2) / 4}$, validating an open conjecture from Montanari and Richard (2014). We get precise expressions for the limiting spectral distribution, deterministic equivalent, phase transition threshold and overlap. The main message is that unfolded symmetric tensors spectrally behave like standard Wigner matrices, up to simple transformations accounting for high-order symmetries. We consider extensions to multiple orthogonal spikes, recursive unfolding and non-square unfolding via disproportionate random matrix theory, leading to an interesting conjectured statistical-computational tradeoff regarding the choice of unfolding: square versus long.

entry.title: A Two-Stage Bayesian Framework for Multi-Fidelity Sequential Updating of Spatial Fragility Fields

link.title: A Two-Stage Bayesian Framework for Multi-Fidelity Sequential Updating of Spatial Fragility Fields

entry.content:
This paper develops a Bayesian framework for updating event-conditioned spatial fragility fields by combining physics-informed priors with incrementally available post-disaster observations. The framework supports sequential refinement of regional vulnerability estimates as additional post-disaster evidence becomes available. The framework reformulates physics-informed fragility estimates into a Probit-Normal (PN) representation that captures aleatory variability and epistemic uncertainty in an analytically tractable form. Stage 1 performs local Bayesian updating by moment-matching PN marginals to Beta surrogates that preserve their probability shapes, enabling conjugate Beta-Bernoulli updates with soft, multi-fidelity observations. Fidelity weights encode source reliability, and the resulting Beta posteriors are re-projected into PN form, producing heteroscedastic fragility estimates whose variances reflect data quality and coverage. Stage 2 assimilates the heteroscedastic pseudo-observations through an ordered probit-warped Gaussian Process (GP) that propagates information across space and structural archetypes. A shared latent spatial severity field and strictly positive threshold-gap functions enforce pathwise ordering of exceedance probabilities and yield nonnegative exact damage-state probabilities. The framework is applied to the 2011 Joplin tornado, where wind-field priors and computer-vision damage assessments are fused under varying assumptions about tornado width, sampling strategy, and observation completeness. Controlled synthetic experiments and the Joplin application show that the framework can reduce the influence of biased priors as evidence accumulates, propagate locally updated information into unobserved regions, and produce uncertainty-aware, ordinally valid exceedance and exact damage-state probability fields.

entry.title: A generalized lasso formulation of weighted and regularized (nearly-)isotonic regression on graphs

link.title: A generalized lasso formulation of weighted and regularized (nearly-)isotonic regression on graphs

entry.content:
In this paper we study a regularized version of nearly-isotonic regression with respect to a general partial order. In this estimator the sum of squares is weighted, with some of the weights allowed to be zero, and an additional quadratic penalty is imposed. The only assumption we make is that the quadratic part of the objective function is strictly convex, and we show that this assumption is mild. First, we show that for all sufficiently large values of the penalty parameter the estimator coincides with the regularized isotonic regression, in which the penalty is replaced by the isotonic constraint. Further, we prove that the resulting problem can be written as a generalized lasso problem with a design matrix of full column rank and with the penalty matrix unchanged. Next, we derive the dual problem, which is a quadratic program with box constraints, and write it in a sparse form that can be solved by standard quadratic programming solvers for sparse problems.

entry.title: Aggregate Calibration Can Mask Stress-State Undercoverage: Bounded-Memory Forecast Intervals under Recurrent Financial Stress

link.title: Aggregate Calibration Can Mask Stress-State Undercoverage: Bounded-Memory Forecast Intervals under Recurrent Financial Stress

entry.content:
Sequential forecast intervals are often evaluated by aggregate coverage even when calibration memory is bounded. This can be misleading when economically important states recur after long absences: a recent-only buffer may satisfy its overall coverage target while no longer containing errors from earlier episodes of the returning state. We study this problem in next-day financial range forecasting, holding the forecasting model, conformity score, adaptive update, and memory budget constant while varying the historical residual information available at each query. Recent-only first-in, first-out (FIFO) calibration is near nominal in aggregate but undercovers substantially during high-volatility states in both an exchange-traded fund development panel and a fixed stock panel. An unbounded state-history reference yields a lower observed stress-period interval score; Rare replay yields lower high-VIX interval scores than the matched Recent-n and Hybrid-n controls in both panels, and the state-structured versus recent-only contrast is largest near stress re-entry. Bounded calibration memory is therefore part of the forecasting information design, and aggregate calibration alone can conceal state-specific reliability failures.

entry.title: Almost Sure Convergence Rates of Stochastic Approximation and Reinforcement Learning via a Poisson-Moreau Drift

link.title: Almost Sure Convergence Rates of Stochastic Approximation and Reinforcement Learning via a Poisson-Moreau Drift

entry.content:
Establishing almost sure convergence rates for stochastic approximation and reinforcement learning under Markovian noise is a fundamental theoretical challenge. We make progress towards this challenge for a class of stochastic approximation algorithms whose expected updates are contractive, a setting that arises in many reinforcement learning algorithms such as $Q$-learning and linear temporal difference learning. Specifically, for a power-law learning rate $O(n^{-\eta})$ with $\eta \in (1/2, 1)$, we obtain an almost sure convergence rate arbitrarily close to $o(n^{1 - 2\eta})$. For the harmonic learning rate $\alpha_n=\alpha/(n+1)$, the almost sure squared-error rate is $o(n^{-\zeta})$ for every $\zeta<\min{1,2(1-\kappa)\alpha}$, where $\kappa$ is the contraction factor. Thus exponents arbitrarily close to one are available when $2(1-\kappa)\alpha\geq1$. This approaches the $n^{-1}$ polynomial exponent of classical law-of-the-iterated-logarithm benchmarks. Key to our analysis is a novel Lyapunov drift construction that applies a Poisson-equation based correction for Markovian noise to the well-established Moreau-envelope smoothing for the contractive mapping.

entry.title: Amortized Nonlinear Variable Selection with Prior-Data Fitted Networks

link.title: Amortized Nonlinear Variable Selection with Prior-Data Fitted Networks

entry.content:
Variable selection is an important task for interpreting potentially complex systems in fields such as biology, business, and sociology. The importance of variable selection has attracted considerable attention in statistics and machine learning. In this paper, we are mainly interested in model-agnostic variable selection for identifying variables that have general nonlinear dependence on the response. We propose MambaPFN, short for Model-Agnostic Markov BlAnket selection with Prior-data Fitted Networks, which is built upon the Transformer, a building block of many popular large language models. Specifically, we consider a functional-mapping perspective on variable-selection learning, in which the Transformer is treated as a learnable mapping from a dataset to its relevant variables. To learn this mapping, MambaPFN introduces three new components: (i) a faithful, rich, and scalable scheme for generating pretraining data, (ii) an objective that targets each variable’s posterior inclusion probability, and (iii) a modified Transformer architecture tailored to variable selection. Once pretrained, MambaPFN is applied to new datasets without parameter updates. Empirically, MambaPFN achieves desirable variable-selection performance in simulation studies and exhibits a scaling law—more pretraining datasets and larger models can continuously improve its performance. Applied to a Facebook comments dataset, MambaPFN selects the fewest variables and achieves the highest computational efficiency and predictive performance, improving upon the best baselines by about 20%.

entry.title: Analytically Calibrated Upper L-Statistics for High-Dimensional Mean Change-Point Testing

link.title: Analytically Calibrated Upper L-Statistics for High-Dimensional Mean Change-Point Testing

entry.content:
This paper develops upper L-statistic methods for testing and localizing a high-dimensional mean change. At each candidate split, the proposed statistics rank the squared studentized CUSUM values across coordinates and aggregate either a fixed number or a fixed proportion of the largest entries. This construction connects max-type and sum-type procedures and provides sensitivity to a wide range of sparsity regimes. We establish asymptotic null distributions under an independent-component representation allowing weak cross-sectional dependence. The limiting laws are Poisson tangent processes for fixed ranks and Gaussian-process or Gumbel laws for proportional ranks. To improve finite-sample performance, we develop analytic calibrations for marginal variance estimation, cross-sectional dependence, extreme clustering, and skewness, and establish their first-order validity. We combine calibrated p-values from a matched pair of fixed- and proportional-order statistics using the Cauchy combination rule to adapt to unknown sparsity. For localization, the estimated change point is selected from the component scan with the smallest p-value. Simulation studies demonstrate generally satisfactory size calibration, competitive detection power, and effective localization across different sparsity levels. An application to semiconductor manufacturing data further illustrates the practical utility of the proposed methods.

entry.title: A new gradient-free active subspace estimation method with application to rare event probability estimation

link.title: A new gradient-free active subspace estimation method with application to rare event probability estimation

entry.content:
To reduce the cost of estimating the probability of a rare event involving a very large number of random parameters, we propose a new strategy for dimension reduction coupled with a surrogate model for the expensive part of the algorithm. To this end, we extend the Ordinary Kriging Active Subspace (OK-AS) method into a sequential version. Our approach consists of iteratively re-estimating the active subspace using a Kriging surrogate trained in a rotated coordinate system until the active subspace stabilises. This method allows for a reduction in prediction error and a better approximation of the active subspace on a benchmark of test problems. Furthermore, we integrate our algorithm into an efficient pre-existing approach for estimating the probability of a rare event. This approach is based on learning the active subspace associated with the random event whose probability is to be estimated. The sequential learning of an importance sampling density is necessary and corresponds to the expensive part of this strategy. To circumvent this issue, we integrate our sequential OK-AS version into the estimation of the importance sampling density. The numerical results indicate that our method allows for reducing the cost required to obtain a precise estimate of the rare event probability.

entry.title: A reliability data aggregation method for fusion-oriented research facilities

link.title: A reliability data aggregation method for fusion-oriented research facilities

entry.content:
This paper aims to develop a statistical method for integrating multiple incomplete data sources to improve the estimation of the failure-rate probability distribution of fusion-specific devices. The data aggregation approach proposed in this work is to support the Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, and Inspectability (RAMI) studies for fusion-oriented research facilities. This work focuses on developing a procedure for handling missing or incomplete data from multiple sources, as well as formulating a statistical framework for combining data from different sources that refer to the same equipment type and failure mode. Specifically, a Bayesian result is adopted under the assumption of a constant failure rate over time. This framework motivates the use of the Gamma distributions to model the failure-rate parameter of each device. Subsequently, two alternative procedures are introduced to approximate, using a single Gamma distribution, the weighted mixture formed by combining Gamma distributions corresponding to the same equipment type across multiple data sources. The proposed method is validated through an extensive simulation study and further illustrated by application to the accelerator systems of the IFMIF-DONES facility. Finally, the proposed algorithm has been implemented in the open-source software R to facilitate its use in the nuclear fusion community.

entry.title: A signal-processing cascade linking satellite heat exposure, genomic variation, and mortality risk

link.title: A signal-processing cascade linking satellite heat exposure, genomic variation, and mortality risk

entry.content:
Heat-related mortality varies among individuals under similar environmental conditions, yet environmental exposure and genetic susceptibility are typically modelled separately. We propose a signal-processing cascade linking satellite-derived land-surface temperature to sequence-dependent heat-shock response and mortality risk. The framework combines distributed-lag filtering of thermal exposure, nonlinear HSF1 activation, cross-correlation with an HSF1 position-weight-matrix kernel, and Hill-model mapping of sequence-dependent binding changes to regulatory response. entry.title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry

link.title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry

entry.content:
Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.

entry.title: A unified approach to outlier identification for mixed-type continuous/ordinal data

link.title: A unified approach to outlier identification for mixed-type continuous/ordinal data

entry.content:
We present an outlier identification method for mixed type data sets comprising continuous and ordinal variables. We define outliers based on using a multivariate Gaussian distribution as reference distribution for non-outliers, with a latent Gaussian assumed for ordinal variables. The proposed algorithm is based on the robust Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator for estimating the parameters of the multivariate Gaussian for the non-outliers. This is extended to account for the fact that the full Gaussian information underlying the ordinal variables is not observed. A breakdown theorem shows that replacing observations will noty stop extreme enough outliers from being identified. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated via simulations on synthetic data with various types of contamination, achieving high detection and low false positive rates. Practical relevance is illustrated through an application to Airbnb listing data containing both continuous and ordinal attributes.

link.title: Axiomatic Learning and Probabilistic Structures with first applications to variants of Arithmetic Machine Learning and beyond

entry.content:
We introduce the Axiomatic Learning Structures (ALS) and Axiomatic Probabilistic Structure (APS) in order to study the interactions of Machine Learning, Optimization, with research frameworks- which, we take the view, can be characterized at the core by the corresponding axioms. The ALS explores the interplays between structures that one is interested in Learning Theory such as Loss functions and the axioms of the objects and transformations involved in these functions. The APS studies the interaction between structures of interest in Probability Theory such as Gibbs distributions, equations with noise, etc. and the axioms of the corresponding objects and transformations. We also introduce in Section 6 Transformations-Axiomatic Based Learning (TABLe) on Mathematical data-sets. One feature of this approach is the ranking of transformations from a table for a certain task based on scores which reflect which transformations work better than others, similarly to when human investigators try various methods on a task. We also study structure recovery from noisy data. In particular, to exemplify the ideas, we consider loss functions which contain derivations and derivations-like transformations. As a first application we study recovery in the context of polynomials with integer coefficients using standard derivatives along with other types of derivations which appear in Arithmetic: the p-derivations which satisfy \textit{different axioms} from the usual derivatives. As a first application of the APS we study a class of noisy (partial/mixed) derivations equations. In the last sections, to provide further potential applications of this framework, we give an overview of an initial simplified Opinion Dynamics model and its (simultaneous) study of rules of updates.

entry.title: BEAGLE in Action: Phylogenetic Likelihoods for Very Large State Spaces

link.title: BEAGLE in Action: Phylogenetic Likelihoods for Very Large State Spaces

entry.content:
Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

entry.title: Bandwidth rules for Dirichlet kernel density estimation on the simplex

link.title: Bandwidth rules for Dirichlet kernel density estimation on the simplex

entry.content:
Dirichlet kernels provide a natural tool for density estimation on the simplex, but data-driven bandwidth selection for them has been mostly limited to likelihood cross-validation (LCV). We develop bandwidth selectors for Dirichlet kernel estimators of densities and projected first derivatives for compositional data. Using a Dirichlet mixture as the reference model, we derive an exact representation of the mean integrated squared error (MISE) and define the exact MISE (EMI) selector. We also derive a closed-form least-squares cross-validation (LSCV) criterion and introduce the reference-smoothed least-squares (RSLS) selector, which replaces the unstable leave-one-out term of LSCV with the fitted Dirichlet mixture. For derivative estimation, we obtain projected derivatives of the Dirichlet density and their integrability conditions, extend the new bandwidth selectors, and carry out kernel mean shift clustering on the simplex. Simulations show that EMI is the most competitive selector for larger samples and Dirichlet-like targets, RSLS generally performs best for small samples and is more stable than LSCV for derivative estimation, and LCV remains competitive for non-Dirichlet targets in density estimation. Applications to wholesale customer expenditure and sectoral employment data illustrate density estimation and clustering, respectively.

entry.title: Bayesian Change-Point Detection and Fault Scoring in District Heating Systems

link.title: Bayesian Change-Point Detection and Fault Scoring in District Heating Systems

entry.content:
Smart heat meter data provide an important basis for monitoring district-heating installations, but fault reports are delayed, incomplete and temporally coarse: a report follows the appearance of a fault, sometimes by weeks, so the onset is unknown. This blurs the distinction between statistical changes and operational faults and prevents the reliable labelling that fault classifiers require. Changepoint detectors such as the Bayesian Estimator of Abrupt Change, Seasonality, and Trend (BEAST) report only the probability that a change occurred, so a large jump and a much smaller one can receive the same probability, and probabilities alone cannot tell a utility which installation to inspect first. We therefore develop a decision score that applies BEAST to temperature difference and flow and scores each detected changepoint by its posterior probability together with its deviation from recent operation, jump size, local behaviour and physical direction. Cases with unfavourable changes in both channels, the pattern of insufficient cooling, receive the highest priority. Of 1,522 cases, 648 had a reported fault; these made up 96% of the 25 highest-priority cases and 90% of the highest 200, and Average Precision was 0.771 against a reported-fault prevalence of 0.426. As cases without a report are not verified to be fault-free, these figures are likely conservative. Without using the report date, the strongest unfavourable flow change in reported-fault cases fell a median of 11 days before the report. Level-based screening of temperature difference, as practised by utilities, ranked the cases comparably but cannot date the change, and the two kinds of evidence were complementary. The method can serve as the first step in a fault-detection workflow, providing a manageable subset of installations for inspection and candidate onset dates for training fault classifiers.

entry.title: Bayesian Cluster-Adjusted Standardised Mean Differences: A Simulation Study

link.title: Bayesian Cluster-Adjusted Standardised Mean Differences: A Simulation Study

entry.content:
Reporting standardised mean differences of continuous psychometric measures is omnipresent in psychology. In a randomised controlled trial with a multilevel structure, one can define a cluster-adjusted version of these quantities naturally taking into account heterogeneous residual variances and accounting for the multilevel structure. In this article, we carefully define the underlying location-scale distributional mixed-effects models and derive cluster-adjusted standardised mean differences using partial pooling. Estimating these quantities is best handled using Bayesian statistics, and we perform an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study to test the performance of these metrics under different simulation configurations. We conclude that in order to measure the a-priori heterogeneous treatment effect across clusters in practically relevant scenarios, it is enough to consider random effects only on the location model and not on the scale model. Even under artificial severe heteroscedasticity, this reduced model performs well both in terms of parameter bias and predictive accuracy. The resulting cluster-adjusted standardised mean difference is an average value across clusters, where the heterogeneity is summarised via its standard deviation.

entry.title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation

link.title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation

entry.content:
Bitcoin perpetual futures trade continuously with shallow liquidity and high price impact, making them prone to millisecond-scale flash crashes. Agent-based limit order book simulators are a natural tool for studying such events, but their behavioral parameters are usually hand-crafted or require full order book histories that are rarely available at scale. We propose a four-stage pipeline that constructs a reproducible 100 ms BTCUSDT flash-crash event panel from 66 detected events, elicits behavioral priors for four agent archetypes using an offline large language model conditioned on empirical microstructure anchors, instantiates a heterogeneous limit order book simulator with the validated priors, and applies causal discovery plus counterfactual analysis to the resulting synthetic panel. Across 500 simulation runs, LLM-elicited priors produce a crash rate of 0.176 versus 0.008 under uninformative uniform priors and generate heav- ier return tails. In the frozen counterfactual analysis, reducing leverage amplification by one within-sample standard deviation lowers the predicted crash rate from 0.176 to 0.136, whereas reducing directional pressure yields only a marginal change. These find- ings suggest that empirically anchored LLM elicitation can improve simulator fidelity and help identify plausible crash-amplification mechanisms in a controlled synthetic environment

entry.title: Beyond Multi-Index Models: Learning Intersections of Degree-2 PTFs

link.title: Beyond Multi-Index Models: Learning Intersections of Degree-2 PTFs

entry.content:
We give an algorithm for PAC learning intersections of $k$ degree-2 polynomial threshold functions over $R^d$ under a Gaussian distribution. Our algorithm achieves classification error $\epsilon$ using $d^{O(k)}2^{O_k(\log^3(1/\epsilon))}$ time and samples, improving over the $d^{O(k^2/\epsilon^2)}$ running time of the polynomial regression approach. To our knowledge, our result is the first to obtain a dimension exponent independent of the accuracy parameter, even for $k=2$. We complement our algorithmic result with an SQ lower bound showing that the complexity dependence of $d^{\Omega(k)}$ is unavoidable. Lifting the input to polynomial features turns the target into an intersection of $k$ halfspaces. This suggests using the first two labeled moments for subspace recovery. In the lifted space, however, these moments can reveal nothing. Our starting point is a Gaussian comparison theorem showing that, for sufficiently regular defining quadratics, the labeled moments needed for subspace recovery are approximately preserved. To handle arbitrary defining quadratics, we establish a new structural result showing that every direction with significant resampling influence can be detected through degree-$O(k)$ moments. These results yield an initial $d^{O(k)}2^{\mathrm{poly}_k(1/\epsilon)}$-time learner using adaptive restrictions. To improve the exponential dependence on $1/\epsilon$, we develop a two-stage dimension-reduction approach that avoids the costly adaptive partitioning. After identifying a subspace containing all directions with large influence, we use generalized regularity and Gaussian comparison to recover the remaining relevant quadratic features through a new derivative-based moment operator. The recovered features support an intersection close to the target. Combining them with robust hinge-loss minimization gives our quasipolynomial-time learner.

entry.title: Bezier-GP: Bezier-Surface-Based Gaussian Process for Chips-on-Wafer Warpage Modeling

link.title: Bezier-GP: Bezier-Surface-Based Gaussian Process for Chips-on-Wafer Warpage Modeling

entry.content:
As the semiconductor industry transitions to the post-Moore paradigm, wafer warpage has become a critical quality issue in advanced packaging; particularly for 3D stacking and high-bandwidth memory manufacturing where die-level deformation can affect bonding quality, interconnect reliability, and yield. However, direct high-throughput measurement of individual chip warpage remains difficult in mass-production environments, while existing wafer-level metrology systems routinely provide dense 3D shape data at the wafer scale. This paper proposes a Bezier-surface-based Gaussian Process—known as Bezier-GP—for chips-on-wafer warpage modeling. The proposed framework combines wafer-level point-cloud metrology data with wafer-map layout information to construct chip-region-level Bezier surface patches, imposes continuity constraints between neighboring patches, and represents the resulting chips-on-wafer surface through a compact free-control-point vector. A GP is then introduced in this low-dimensional representation to model wafer-to-wafer variation, chip-region-level spatial dependence, and provide uncertainty quantification. Numerical experiments, using an ASC wafer-map layout, demonstrate that the proposed framework can reconstruct chips-on-wafer surfaces, preserve chip-region-level geometric interpretability, and recover population-level mean and covariance structures under a controlled multi-wafer simulation setting. The results suggest that Bezier-GP provides a measurement-driven statistical modeling foundation for connecting wafer-level metrology data to chip-region-level warpage analysis in semiconductor manufacturing.

entry.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series

link.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series

entry.content:
The self-controlled case series (SCCS) design is widely used in studies of rare events, for example of vaccine side effects. Conceptually, the design has two main features. First, it requires only data from individuals who have experienced the event of interest. Therefore, the design is especially useful when the outcome is rare and the available data come from surveillance or clinical records, say, of hospitalized patients. Second, because comparisons are made within single individuals, time-invariant confounding between treatment and outcome is eliminated. We formulate a set of sufficient identification assumptions for estimating the causal effect of vaccination on an adverse outcome under the SCCS design, drawing on ideas from the causal inference literature. Unlike the existing SCCS literature, we do not consider a parametric model as the starting point. This allows us to establish when and why the SCCS design allows identification of causal effects, using data from cases only. However, because the sufficient identifiability assumptions are implausible in some applications, we also develop statistical tests for the existence of a treatment effect that remain valid when only a subset of the identification assumptions holds.

entry.title: Conditional independence and graphical models for rankings

link.title: Conditional independence and graphical models for rankings

entry.content:
Ranking models define probability distributions over rankings and are fundamental in applications such as preference learning and decision-making. Without structural assumptions, these models are intractable due to their factorial complexity. Although independence assumptions are key to reducing complexity and enabling interpretability, standard notions of conditional independence must account for the mutual exclusivity constraints inherent to rankings. We introduce relative rank models, a probabilistic framework based on structured coarsenings of the ranking space that relax these constraints while preserving relative order information. This representation enables a well-defined notion of conditional independence for rankings and allows rankings to be modeled using Bayesian networks. As a result, standard methods for learning and probabilistic inference can be applied to rankings, with interpretable representations based on conditional independence. We further show that two prominent ranking models based on independence assumptions tailored to rankings arise as special cases, providing a unifying framework for independence in ranking models.

entry.title: Conformal prediction regions for dependent censored lifetimes

link.title: Conformal prediction regions for dependent censored lifetimes

entry.content:
Joint-life insurance and annuity benefits depend on two or more dependent lifetimes, which portfolio data observe only up to a valuation date. Given the covariates of a new contract, such as the entry ages of a couple, we construct one lower bound per remaining lifetime such that, with at least a prespecified probability, every life survives beyond its bound. The first step is to characterize the functions which allow for a useful projection from a multivariate to a univariate setting. The construction then relies on univariate conformal prediction, which calibrates any fitted model on held-out data, so that this statement does not rely on a correct mortality or dependence model. Censoring is handled by calibrating on the contracts observed for at least a fixed horizon, weighted by the inverse of their probability of being observed that long. We show that, when the lives can be censored at different times, this is possible precisely for joint statements that every life survives beyond its own bound, and that a common censoring time also permits bounds on the second-death time. If censoring is independent of the lifetimes given the covariates, coverage holds for every sample size when these probabilities are known, and approximately in large samples when they or the conditional lifetime quantiles are estimated consistently. As an application, we analyze a Canadian joint-life annuity portfolio.

entry.title: Covariate Adjustment for Time-Restricted Marginal Win Statistics in Randomized Trials: Assumption-Lean Inference and Guaranteed Efficiency Gain

link.title: Covariate Adjustment for Time-Restricted Marginal Win Statistics in Randomized Trials: Assumption-Lean Inference and Guaranteed Efficiency Gain

entry.content:
Hierarchical composite endpoints, analyzed through win statistics such as the net benefit (NB), win ratio (WR), and win odds (WO), are increasingly used in randomized trials to prioritize endpoints according to clinical importance. Although covariate-adjustment methods for win statistics have been developed, a unified model-assisted approach for mixed-type, time-restricted HCEs with simultaneous asymptotic no-loss efficiency guarantees remains of interest. We propose a unified, model-assisted covariate-adjustment framework for time-restricted marginal win statistics evaluated at a prespecified post-randomization restriction horizon, a clinically interpretable estimand particularly suited to acute and high-acuity trials with well-defined short-term follow-up windows. The Hoeffding–H’ajek projection of the two-sample win–loss U-statistics yields subject-level influence functions for the marginal win and loss probabilities. We apply treatment-specific linear covariate adjustment to these influence functions and propagate the adjustment to NB, log WR, and log WO. The resulting estimators are assumption-lean, remaining consistent and asymptotically valid without correct specification of the linear working model, and are asymptotically guaranteed efficiency gain over their unadjusted counterparts. Simulations with mixed-type HCEs demonstrate substantial efficiency and power gains with prognostic covariate adjustment. However, including additional non-prognostic covariates can impair finite-sample variance estimation and inflate Type I error, particularly in smaller trials. Bootstrap variance estimation improved inferential calibration in these settings. We illustrate the proposed method using a randomized acute kidney injury alert trial.

entry.title: Data-Efficient Kernel Methods for Learning Differential Equations and Their Solution Operators: Algorithms and Error Analysis

link.title: Data-Efficient Kernel Methods for Learning Differential Equations and Their Solution Operators: Algorithms and Error Analysis

entry.content:
We introduce a novel kernel-based framework for learning differential equations and their solution maps. The framework is efficient in its data requirements in terms of the number of observed states and the amount of data available per state. Our formulation also allows us to employ efficient Gauss-Newton-type optimization algorithms in the training procedure to improve accuracy and speed of the training procedure. We also support our algorithm with rigorous theoretical guarantees in the form of quantitative worst-case error bounds for the learned equation that can be extended to the subsequent solution operators under smoothness assumptions. Numerical benchmarks demonstrate significant improvements in computational complexity and robustness while achieving one to two orders of magnitude improvements in terms of accuracy compared to certain state-of-the-art algorithms.

entry.title: Debiased Estimating Equation Method for Robust and Efficient Mendelian Randomization Using a Large Number of Correlated Weak and Invalid Instruments

link.title: Debiased Estimating Equation Method for Robust and Efficient Mendelian Randomization Using a Large Number of Correlated Weak and Invalid Instruments

entry.content:
Mendelian randomization (MR) is a widely used tool for causal inference in the presence of unmeasured confounders, which uses single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) as instrumental variables to estimate causal effects. However, SNPs often have weak effects on complex traits, leading to bias in existing MR analyses when weak instruments are included. In addition, existing MR methods often restrict analysis to independent SNPs via linkage disequilibrium clumping and result in a loss of efficiency in estimating the causal effect due to discarding correlated SNPs. To address these issues, we propose the Debiased Estimating Equation Method (DEEM), a summary statistics-based MR approach that can incorporate a large number of correlated, weak-effect, and invalid SNPs. DEEM effectively eliminates the weak instrument bias and improves the statistical efficiency of the causal effect estimation by leveraging information from a large number of correlated SNPs. DEEM also allows for pleiotropic effects, adjusts for the winner’s curse, and applies to both two-sample and one-sample MR analyses. Asymptotic analyses of the DEEM estimator demonstrate its attractive theoretical properties. Through extensive simulations and two real data examples, we demonstrate that DEEM significantly improves the efficiency and robustness of MR analysis compared with existing methods.

entry.title: Decentralized Sparse Quantile Regression

link.title: Decentralized Sparse Quantile Regression

entry.content:
Distributed statistical learning has recently attracted significant attention owing to its computational efficiency and scalability in large-scale systems. However, the non-smooth quantile loss poses substantial challenges to the development of efficient decentralized algorithms for quantile regression. Existing methods may either suffer from slow convergence or rely on smoothing-based approximations that require additional stringent assumptions, particularly in high-dimensional settings. To address these issues, we propose a decentralized framework that integrates gradient tracking with iterative hard thresholding for sparse quantile estimation. The proposed method avoids smoothing approximations and relaxes the initialization requirement. Theoretically, we show that the proposed algorithm achieves linear convergence under stated regularity conditions and that the resulting estimator attains the same order of statistical accuracy as its centralized counterpart. We further develop a decentralized information criterion for selecting the working sparsity level and establish support screening guarantees. Numerical experiments and a real-data study illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed method.

entry.title: Deep Learning of Compositional Targets with Hierarchical Spectral Methods

link.title: Deep Learning of Compositional Targets with Hierarchical Spectral Methods

entry.content:
Why depth yields a computational advantage over shallow methods remains a central open question in learning theory. We study this question in a controlled high-dimensional Gaussian setting, focusing on compositional target functions. We analyze their learnability using an explicit three-layer fitting model trained via layer-wise spectral estimators. The target combines polynomial latent features with a scalar readout, and its compositional structure allows learning to proceed in stages. Recovering an intermediate representation reduces the problem to lower-degree spectral estimation tasks, as in multi-index models. Our analysis establishes Gaussian comparison bounds for projected moments when $0<\varepsilon<1/3$, and motivates separations in sample complexity between two- and three-layer learning strategies, conditional on a conjectured spectral recovery step.

entry.title: Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models

link.title: Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models

entry.content:
We study score learning from denoising pairs when the data contain a hidden non-Gaussian component. If covariance reveals the component, its subspace can be recovered directly. If covariance is isotropic, the first distinguishing moment has order $k^\ast$, and the learner must extract that moment from clean points and their noisy views. Correlations in the denoising loss are Stein discrepancies against a baseline; for polynomial fields they determine exactly the corresponding moment differences. Averaging fresh noisy views conditional on a clean point gives an exact moment query on the clean distribution. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an $L^4/L^2$ condition need order $d^{k^\ast-1}$ features, and the stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples. Small-step online SGD on one unit has this exponent up to logarithms. A two-stage learner uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss to recover the hidden direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For every even $k^\ast$, it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from $O(d^{k^\ast/2}\log d)$ clean points. In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold occurs at $d^J/J!$, while projection onto principal components makes the fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension. In the covariance-matched experiments, the measured partial-trace overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a $d^2$-like training-set threshold over $d=64$–$192$, with fixed validation and calibration overhead.

entry.title: Descending Everest, Part II: Oracle Complexity of Minimizing a Sum of Convex $(L_0,L_1)$-Smooth Functions

link.title: Descending Everest, Part II: Oracle Complexity of Minimizing a Sum of Convex $(L_0,L_1)$-Smooth Functions

entry.content:
We study the minimization of the average of $n$ convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions: the Hessian norm of each function is bounded by an affine function of its gradient norm. We assume known upper bounds $R$ on the distance from the starting point to a minimizer and $\delta$ on the difference between the minimum of the average and the average of the infima of the components. We derive upper and lower bounds on the oracle complexity of reaching accuracy $\varepsilon$ in function value in expectation. Up to logarithmic factors, both bounds are of order $n(1+(L_1R)^{2/3}) +\sqrt{\frac{n(L_0+L_1^2\delta)R^2}{\varepsilon}+n(L_1R)^2}$. The upper bound is attained by the proposed method YETI. The method combines ideas of accelerated proximal methods and variance reduction methods with a heuristic for choosing additional points. The number of oracle calls made by the heuristic is bounded, which preserves the upper bound on the total number of queries needed to reach the target accuracy. In the experiments, YETI is compared with first-order methods on synthetic problems and Poisson regression problems. We also examine the stopping criterion and the effect of the heuristic separately. The lower bound is obtained by an explicit construction of families of instances that are hard for any first-order method.

entry.title: Deterministic Uniformization for Estimation and Latent Trajectory Inference in Interval-Censored Multistate Triansition Models

link.title: Deterministic Uniformization for Estimation and Latent Trajectory Inference in Interval-Censored Multistate Triansition Models

entry.content:
Interval-censored multistate data arise when subjects are observed at irregular visit times, leaving transition times and intermediate states unobserved. Likelihood-based inference for continuous-time Markov models often requires computationally intensive matrix exponential evaluations. We propose a deterministic uniformization expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm for parameter estimation and latent trajectory inference. By representing the continuous-time process through an embedded Markov chain indexed by latent Poisson event counts, the method enables deterministic E-step calculations without repeated matrix exponential evaluations. The M-step reduces to transition-specific Poisson regressions with exposure offsets, accommodating covariate-dependent transition intensities. We establish uniform truncation error bounds and show that the procedure is an asymptotically monotone generalized EM algorithm. Under standard regularity conditions, the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Simulations demonstrate accurate estimation and computational advantages over direct likelihood optimization, particularly for complex transition structures. We also develop an exact dynamic programming method to calculate posterior probabilities of candidate latent pathways and identify the most probable pathway between observations. Posterior expected transition counts and state occupancy times provide additional subject-specific summaries, while expected-count ratios offer a computational shortcut for classification in simple mutually exclusive pathway structures. The framework supports both population-level inference and individualized characterization of disease progression.

entry.title: Development of tools for all-cause mortality prediction in heart failure patients: a systematic review

link.title: Development of tools for all-cause mortality prediction in heart failure patients: a systematic review

entry.content:
Heart failure is a serious medical condition associated with risk of acute deterioration, recurrent hospitalizations and high mortality making accurate mortality prediction potentially valuable for patient care and healthcare planning. Numerous prognostic models have been developed using conventional statistics (CS), machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), but variation in study populations, heart failure definitions, prediction horizons and development practices may limit interpretation of applicability. We conducted a systematic review of mortality prediction models published between 2009 to the start of 2026 searching three databases (PubMed, IEEE and Scopus) for studies predicting all-cause mortality over a 1-60 months prediction horizon among patients with heart failure. Data extracted were cohort characteristics, heart failure definitions, model development, cohort size, validation practices, mortality, computational model design and reported performance. The risk of bias and applicability were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Of 1516 publications identified, 56 met the inclusion criteria. Publication numbers increased over the observation period, alongside increasing use of ML/DL models and decreasing use of CS approaches. Most development cohorts (64%) were classified as Unknown/Undefined heart failure, reflecting inconsistent reporting and terminology that did not correspond with established heart failure guidelines. External validation was reported in 23% of studies. Overall, research in modeling heart failure mortality has grown alongside increasing adoption of ML/DL approaches. Greater standardization of study design and reporting is needed for meaningful comparison, reproducibility and evaluation of models for clinical application.

entry.title: Directional Statistics in Signal Processing: A Geometry Driven Overview of Models, Learning, and Applications

link.title: Directional Statistics in Signal Processing: A Geometry Driven Overview of Models, Learning, and Applications

entry.content:
Many signal-processing objects are defined by periodicity, normalization, sign or global-phase ambiguity, basis invariance, or positive-semidefinite constraints and therefore cannot be modeled faithfully in ordinary Euclidean space. This paper develops a geometry driven framework for directional statistics in signal processing, connecting signal representations to their natural manifolds or quotient spaces and to probability models compatible with their invariances. After reviewing instances of directional statistics in the signal processing literature, we review circular, toroidal, spherical, projective, Stiefel, Grassmann, and covariance-valued distributions, emphasizing their statistical assumptions, computational requirements, and dimensional limitations relevant to signal processing. We describe various modeling and estimation strategies, including analytical and gradient-based maximum likelihood, structured low-rank parameterizations, mixtures and hidden Markov models (HMMs), score-based and contrastive estimation, and geometry-aware K-means. To exemplify the consequences of geometry-aware modeling, we study multivariate phase coherence in synthetic data and functional neuroimaging, comparing toroidal phase vectors to projective, Grassmann, and positive-semidefinite representations. We also study speaker separation in a car environment, showing that directional representations outperform a standard Euclidean model. These examples demonstrate that when the geometric representation, statistical distribution, inference method, and computational regime are considered together, they have the potential to lead to improved models across a broad range of signal processing applications.

entry.title: Efficient Robust Learning at the Information-Theoretic Limit

link.title: Efficient Robust Learning at the Information-Theoretic Limit

entry.content:
In an important recent work, Blanc (2026) gave an algorithm for robustly learning Boolean concept classes with respect to a fixed distribution that outputs a (randomized) classifier achieving the optimal error of $\eta + \varepsilon$ where $\eta$ is the noise rate. In contrast, it is well known that deterministic hypotheses cannot achieve error less than $2\eta + \varepsilon.$ Blanc’s algorithm is computationally inefficient, and the main problem left open in his work is to find a polynomial-time algorithm given access to an oracle for empirical risk minimization (ERM). In this paper, we resolve this problem and give such an algorithm. Perhaps surprisingly, our techniques make crucial use of various types of no-regret learners. Additionally, we give an efficient algorithm (no ERM oracle required) for robustly learning any function class that admits sandwiching polynomials with respect to hypercontractive distributions. As one consequence, we give the first polynomial-time algorithm for robustly learning a halfspace with respect to Gaussian marginals that achieves error $\eta + \varepsilon$ for any constant $\varepsilon$.

entry.title: Emergence of Distortions in High-Dimensional Guided Diffusion Models

link.title: Emergence of Distortions in High-Dimensional Guided Diffusion Models

entry.content:
Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is the de facto standard for conditional sampling in diffusion models, yet it often reduces sample diversity. Using tools from statistical physics, we analyze the emergence of generative distortions induced by CFG, namely the mismatch between the CFG sampling distribution and the true conditional distribution. We study this phenomenon in analytically tractable settings with exact score functions, characterizing its dependence on data dimensionality and the number of classes. For high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures, we use dynamic mean-field theory to show that distortions persist when the number of classes scales exponentially with the data dimension, whereas they vanish in the sub-exponential regime due to a dynamical phase transition. Moreover we found that, in the infinite-class limit, distortions remain unavoidable regardless of dimensionality because of the increasing density of classes. Finally, we show that standard CFG schedules cannot prevent variance shrinkage, and we propose a theoretically grounded guidance schedule incorporating a negative-guidance window that improves both class separability and sample diversity in real-world latent diffusion models.

link.title: Enabling risk and reliability analysis in next-generation computational tools via multifidelity methods

entry.content:
Risk and reliability analysis are fundamental to the design, assessment, and operation of safety-critical complex systems; however, their integration into next-generation computational tools is constrained by the cost of uncertainty quantification with expensive computational models. The computational challenge is particularly prohibitive for tail-sensitive quantities, such as probabilities of failure, conditional values-at-risk, and buffered probabilities of failure, where accurate estimation can require a large number of model evaluations. Multifidelity methods provide a framework for addressing this computational bottleneck by combining information from models of varying accuracy and cost while retaining the predictive accuracy of the high-fidelity model. This review summarizes the state of the art in methods that enable scalable risk and reliability analysis using multifidelity control variates, multifidelity importance sampling, and multifidelity active learning.

entry.title: Estimating Treatment Effects with a Single Arm Clinical Trial and Data Summaries from an External Control Group: is it Possible?

link.title: Estimating Treatment Effects with a Single Arm Clinical Trial and Data Summaries from an External Control Group: is it Possible?

entry.content:
Randomized controlled trials are crucial for assessing new treatments, but they are often infeasible due to ethical or practical constraints. In these cases, single-arm trials combined with external control data constitute an alternative approach for estimating treatment effects. However, individual patient-level data on external controls are frequently inaccessible due to privacy and economic concerns. Therefore, investigators rely on data summaries published by previous studies of the control therapy. We propose a method for inference on the treatment effect of an experimental therapy using patient-level data from a single-arm trial and a few published data summaries from an external control group. We introduce and study the Interval of Potential Effects (IPE), described as the range of plausible levels of the treatment effect that are compatible with the patient-level data from the experimental treatment and the available summaries on the control group. The width of the IPE quantifies the uncertainty on the treatment effect attributable to the lack of individual patient data from the control group. We demonstrate, through simulations and a case study, how the IPE indicates whether the available summaries are sufficient for accurate estimation of the treatment effect. We also illustrate that IPEs can support decision-making in the early phases of development of new treatments.

entry.title: Estimating the expected output of wide random MLPs more efficiently than sampling

link.title: Estimating the expected output of wide random MLPs more efficiently than sampling

entry.content:
By far the most common way to estimate an expected loss in machine learning is to draw samples, compute the loss on each one, and take the empirical average. However, sampling is not necessarily optimal. Given an MLP at initialization, we show how to estimate its expected output over Gaussian inputs without running samples through the network at all. Instead, we produce approximate representations of the distributions of activations at each layer, leveraging tools such as cumulants and Hermite expansions. We show both theoretically and empirically that for sufficiently wide networks, our estimator achieves a target mean squared error using substantially fewer FLOPs than Monte Carlo sampling. We find moreover that our methods perform particularly well at estimating the probabilities of rare events, and additionally demonstrate how they can be used for model training. Together, these findings suggest a path to producing models with a greatly reduced probability of catastrophic tail risks.

entry.title: Exact Selective Inference for Spectral Clustering via Piecewise-Constant Graph Perturbation

link.title: Exact Selective Inference for Spectral Clustering via Piecewise-Constant Graph Perturbation

entry.content:
Cluster labels are often used twice: first to discover groups, and then to test whether the discovered groups differ. This double use of the data makes ordinary two-sample $p$-values anti-conservative. Selective inference fixes this by conditioning on the clustering event, but for spectral clustering the event appears difficult because the algorithm combines an affinity map, an eigendecomposition, and a rounding step. We show that, for spectral clustering based on unweighted $\varepsilon$- or $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs, the obstruction is the affinity construction rather than the eigendecomposition. Along the one-dimensional perturbation used by the truncated-$\chi$ selective test, graph changes occur only at finitely many real roots of data-dependent quadratic distance comparisons. Between these breakpoints, the graph, Laplacian spectrum, embedding, rounding, and reported cluster pair are deterministic functions of a finite graph state. Consequently, in real arithmetic and under a known-scale spherical Gaussian model, the selection set is an exact finite union of intervals, yielding finite-sample selective $p$-values for selected spectral-cluster pairs. The same argument gives feature-wise truncated-normal tests. We also record direct extensions to known feature covariance, eigengap-selected $K$, and auxiliary-coordinate graphs. We validate null and partial-null calibration, operational power, numerical sensitivity, and model-scope diagnostics, and give a working-model PBMC algorithmic illustration. Smooth kernels such as RBF affinities fall outside the finite-state guarantee.

entry.title: Exact association-test distributions for prior-informed stepwise SNP prioritization

link.title: Exact association-test distributions for prior-informed stepwise SNP prioritization

entry.content:
Prioritizing causal variants in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) is challenging due to linkage disequilibrium and high dimensionality. We propose an iterative algorithm for the selection of genetic variables that allows the integration of biological priors. The proposed algorithm requires the specification of the power function of a test statistic and incorporates a priori information on each SNP. We derive the approximate and exact distributions of several commonly used test statistics. At each step of the proposed algorithm, we select the SNP with the largest a posteriori probability of being causal. We consider several stopping criteria for the algorithm. We conduct comprehensive simulation studies to assess the performance of several versions of the proposed algorithm and to make a comparison to some existing competitors. The use of the proposed prioritization algorithm is illustrated with a cis-eQTL application to a human gene-expression data, using European discovery and Yoruba cross-population replication.

entry.title: Experimentally Validated Digital Twins: Evaluating Workforce Training Programs in the Age of Big Data

link.title: Experimentally Validated Digital Twins: Evaluating Workforce Training Programs in the Age of Big Data

entry.content:
Modern program evaluation prioritizes evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) because prior research found that observational estimates of program impacts often diverge substantially from experimental benchmarks. We revisit this finding — which was based on small survey datasets — in the era of large-scale administrative data. Using anonymized income tax records covering all American adults between 1999 and 2025, we estimate the effects of workforce training programs on earnings by using machine learning models to predict counterfactuals from rich data on prior work histories, demographics, and residential locations. Rather than testing whether our observational estimates are unbiased, we use 37 RCTs to estimate the distribution of their bias. We find that our machine learning estimates closely match the RCT estimates, with root mean squared error (RMSE) comparable to that of the RCTs themselves. Our method reduces RMSE by 60% relative to parametric estimators used in prior work because our larger samples and richer covariates permit more flexible, higher-dimensional models of the counterfactual. Applying our method to a broader set of sites and enrollment years beyond the experimental sample, we find that treatment effects on earnings vary substantially across locations and over time, even within a given program. Programs that place more participants into target-sector jobs generate the largest earnings gains, with impacts that persist even after participants leave their initial jobs. These findings provide guidance for improving job training programs and, more broadly, illustrate a scalable approach to program evaluation that uses observational data to construct experimentally validated ``digital twins.’’

entry.title: Few-Step Boltzmann Generators via Scalable Likelihood Flow Maps

link.title: Few-Step Boltzmann Generators via Scalable Likelihood Flow Maps

entry.content:
Recent progress in flow-based generative modeling has led to models that output high-quality samples while using only a small number of function evaluations. However, at present, there is a lack of similar advances in estimating the model likelihood. In particular, most existing methods either rely on restrictive architectures that enable exact calculations, or use stochastic approximations such as Hutchinson’s trace estimator that introduce substantial variance. In this work, we introduce SCAlable LikeLihood distillation of flOw maPs (SCALLOP). SCALLOP builds on the recently proposed F2D2, a likelihood flow map model that can generate samples and their densities in a small number of function evaluations. While F2D2 uses Hutchinson’s estimator during training, we introduce an alternative and more scalable likelihood distillation objective that is Hutchinson-free and admits a vectorized formulation. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SCALLOP as a Boltzmann generator in molecular science, and further validate its benefit on image datasets. SCALLOP significantly reduces both training variance and training time while consistently improving performance compared to F2D2, and is competitive with the state-of-the-art while achieving up to 10x inference speedup over the fastest baseline.

entry.title: Four Extensions of the Universal Law of Robustness: Log-Concave Covariates, Heterogeneous Mixtures, Vector-Valued Predictors, and Markovian Data

link.title: Four Extensions of the Universal Law of Robustness: Log-Concave Covariates, Heterogeneous Mixtures, Vector-Valued Predictors, and Markovian Data

entry.content:
Bubeck and Sellke’s universal law of robustness says that fitting $n$ noisy samples below the noise level with a class of $p$ real parameters forces a Lipschitz constant of order $\sqrt{nd/p}$, when the covariate distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is isoperimetric: smooth interpolation costs a factor $d$ of overparametrization. Its hypotheses are Gaussian-type concentration, a homogeneous covariate law, scalar outputs, and independent samples; we relax each one. Exponential concentration suffices, at the unchanged rate and absolute constant and at the price of a capacity burn-in, some form of which we show is necessary; this gives the law for normalized log-concave covariates, with a $\log d$ loss from the current KLS bound. For heterogeneous mixtures the worst component constant is replaced by the weighted average of the component constants, under a typicality condition on the mixture composition. For vector-valued predictors the bound at the Frobenius Lipschitz scale is free of the output dimension $K$, and the Euclidean bound loses only $K^{-1/2}$, a loss that covariate-independent noise removes. Stationary Markov covariates retain the i.i.d. rate, the pseudo-spectral gap entering only the sample-size conditions. One master theorem carries the shared argument, and constants are explicit throughout.

link.title: Global Test of Functional Effects in Mean Field Variational Bayesian Scalar-on-Function Regression

entry.content:
Variational regression methods are increasingly popular because they enable efficient estimation in complex statistical models. To characterize their theoretical properties, researchers have established frequentist properties for models fitted using mean-field variational Bayes (MFVB). Finally, we conduct a simulation study comparing our estimation procedure and global test with fully frequentist and fully Bayesian alternatives in terms of bias, root mean squared error, size, and power.

entry.title: Graph-Localized Coverage for Conformal Prediction on Inductive Graphs

link.title: Graph-Localized Coverage for Conformal Prediction on Inductive Graphs

entry.content:
Conformal prediction (CP) provides marginal coverage guarantees, but marginal coverage does not determine where prediction errors occur on a graph. Queries from different graph neighborhoods can exhibit substantially different levels of uncertainty even when aggregate coverage remains near its target. We introduce GLocalCP, an online CP framework for inductive node classification and edge prediction that combines marginal and graph-local calibration with uncertainty-adaptive prediction sets. Specifically, GLocalCP puts forth a novel uncertainty-adaptive nonconformality score that relies on the mutual information obtained from Monte-Carlo (MC) dropout based prediction. Then, it augments a global online threshold with a kernel-based local correction that propagates coverage feedback among similar graph queries. On the theoretical horizon, we establish pathwise $O(N^{-1/2})$ marginal calibration error without exchangeability or stationarity and, for the exact-kernel formulation, an explicit $O(N^{-1/2})$ graph-localized calibration guarantee. Experiments on seven node-classification and seven edge-prediction benchmarks show that similar marginal coverage can conceal substantially different local reliability. Our proposed GLocalCP maintains coverage near the target while consistently reducing graph-local calibration error. Uncertainty scaling in GLocalCP further reduces prediction-set size across all evaluated node and edge datasets while leaving marginal coverage essentially unchanged.

entry.title: How Deep Are Deep GPs, Really? A Sharp Threshold and a Non-Gaussian Limit for Compositional GPs

link.title: How Deep Are Deep GPs, Really? A Sharp Threshold and a Non-Gaussian Limit for Compositional GPs

entry.content:
Compositional priors describe the generic properties of layered functions in deep Bayesian models, where deep neural networks with random weights are a canonical example. In the wide-network limit, the prior is a Gaussian process (GP) with a depth-dependent kernel, and its behaviour as depth grows has been extensively studied through this kernel. Here, we study another case, where each layer itself is a vector valued Gaussian process, and our aim is similarly to understand the limiting behaviour of the prior as depth grows. Previous GP work has established that for the radial basis function (RBF) kernel and a certain range of bandwidths $r$, the prior degenerates in the limit, converging to the set of constant functions, which is not useful as a probabilistic model. In this paper we establish several new results. First, we identify a sharp bandwidth threshold $r_c(d) = \Theta(\sqrt{d})$ above which the limit is degenerate, strengthening the earlier bounds. Second, and more importantly, we show that for $r$ below the threshold $r_c(d)$ the prior converges to a limit distribution $\pi_{\bar{Z}}$. We also prove that these distributions are non-degenerate and non-Gaussian, with non-vanishing dependence between coordinates. In contrast to the previously known degenerate regime, deep Gaussian process priors can therefore admit non-trivial limits. Empirically, we verify the threshold across a range of dimensions $d$, and demonstrate a complex multimodal behaviour of the limit distributions $\pi_{\bar{Z}}$, a regime that becomes increasingly narrow with $d$ and would be hard to identify without knowing the threshold.

entry.title: How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy?

link.title: How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy?

entry.content:
Data-driven algorithms are ubiquitous across industries, and there is an extensive literature on analyzing their \emph{average} performance. The risk profile of such algorithms, while critical, is much less understood. This paper quantifies the risk of data-driven policies and isolates its sources. We evaluate a policy through the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of its loss over the training sample, any policy randomization, and the future outcome, at a fixed unknown distribution. Regret against an oracle that knows the distribution decomposes into expected post-sample regret (PS), the average outcome-only CVaR gap of the selected action, and a sample-risk premium (SR), the additional tail risk omitted by averaging those evaluations. The analogous premium vanishes under expected loss. We characterize when the premium vanishes and how large it is relative to post-sample regret. For losses with a continuous density near the tail cutoff, we identify conditions under which both components decay at the same rate, yet the limiting ratio of the premium to post-sample regret can reach the thousands. When a probability mass at the cutoff moves with the action, the premium can decay more slowly and dominate post-sample regret. We establish conditions under which sample average approximation learns the oracle action at rate $n^{-1/2}$ in both settings, but its combined-risk regret is of order $n^{-1}$ in the first and $n^{-1/2}$ in the second. In finite-sample numerical examples of SAA in both settings, the premium accounts for approximately $74\%$–$97\%$ of regret.
